ROBBERIES GONE EXPLOSIVE

By: Nicky Troll | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
A new crime trend using EXPLOSIVES in cash robberies across SA see criminals making off with over R100 million just 6 months.

Summary:
Robbers are upping their game and turning to new ammo to crack cash management systems with even bigger bounties. Syndicates have moved from hitting ATMs to cash safes and actual cash-in-transit vehicles. With these new targets, a the black market for commercial explosives has been created.
We cast the spotlight a new crime trend, showing just how easy it is to get your hands on explosives.

Further information:
HISTORY
During the days of Stander bank robbers pulled of armed robberies that mirrored scenes from movies. Banks upped their security and crooks turned to ATM bombings.
TODAY
Explosives are being used widely across SA to break into cash management systems like safes, ATMs and even cash in transit vehicles – yes! Cash-in-Transit vehicles. There have 8 in the last few months and it seems to be fast becoming the newest MO. The explosives being used are commercial grade used for mining and above ground blasting – there is a growing black market for these explosives.
FOOTAGE
I have great footage of criminals blowing up safes armed with rifles and explosives – working on getting the only video clip of cash-in-transit robbery.
UNDERCOVER OPERATION
We show how easy it is get your hands on explosives in the black market (have a PI with an informant working on this element).
It’s in Nelspruit – and will require a research trip
WHO IS TO BLAME? THE POLICE….
Five years ago, new legislation was passed tightening up on explosives controls making it the responsibility of the SAPS – but it has yet to be implemented or policed – industry insiders say it's a free for all.

Press Release:


Cash Crimes
Aggravated robbery is up by a whopping 8.5% according to the 2015 crime stats released this week. Business robberies are up by 3.2%. But perhaps it’s not all that surprising. In a new trend, criminals are using commercial explosives to blow open cash safes and cash-in-transit vans. This modus operandi has already netted them over R150-million in just one year. But why is it so easy for criminals to lay their hands on deadly commercial explosives? Carte Blanche blows this investigation wide open.


Script:


STRUCTURE


VO: There are 147 aggravated robberies every day in South Africa. Organised criminal syndicates are going for the big bucks!

Armed with black market explosives they crack cash management systems in double quick time. It’s costing the economy millions of rands in a string of brazen attacks across the country.

BARBARA: These are professionals because they don’t spend a lot of time here. They just dig those holes for the explosives and then few seconds it blows, they come back, take the cash and run away.

VO: Kevin Twiname, from SABRIC, says the use of explosives in cash crime is becoming the norm.

KEVIN: Where there is going to be cash, you are probably going to get explosives, whether it be a safe, a drop safe, whether it be a CIT vehicle or an ATM, the fact is where cash is housed in bulk is what they are after.

VO: Barbara Ngomane manages a petrol station in Gauteng – they have already been hit three times by criminals using this tactic.

BARBARA: The first time it was +/- R45000 // the second time they went away with a R105 000. // the third time, they went away with R76000. CAM A INT 1 M10

VO: But that doesn’t include the resultant damage to the shop and loss of revenue.

KEVIN: The damage caused is irrelevant to them – sometimes the damage caused is by far great than the value of the money.

VO: The Cash-in-Transit industry is big business – it’s money on the road… every day; every where; and criminals want in…

LINK: Now these brazen criminals have set their sights on even bigger targets... they’re going for these... armoured Cash trucks!

VO: In the last year there’s been a dramatic increase in Cash-in-Transit attacks using explosives.

UP FROM just 1 in 2013, to 6 in 2014, and already 11 in 2015.

A trend that is cause for concern says Lt Robert Netshiunda.

ROBERT: We are having sleepless nights knowing there are people having explosives, we don't know what next they are going to blast. INT 1 M20

Nathi is an informant, while he operates in the criminal underworld, he also sells information to industry investigators. Bigger targets mean bigger bounties – criminals also have costs to cover.

INFORMANT: you can’t go and bomb an ATM that has R30 000 in side, you need a stolen vehicle, you need rifles, so that when the police comes to respond, then you shoot them and then you need also to go to a witch doctor to wash... you know us black people, we go and check if our job is going to be fine. We end up costing R20 000 for R30 000. So I mean it’s worthless.

LINK: There have been 12 cash in transit robberies involving explosives in the past year, now it doesn’t sound like a lot, but when you count the money, you’re looking at over R150 million.

VO: A knock the security industry has to take. All major cash-in-transit companies in South Africa have been victims of this new tactic. Wahl Bartmann is the CEO of one the biggest players.

WAHL: The losses can be quite big, but not only on as an industry, but on the economy – it’s got a huge impact.

VO: Sam, an industry investigator says it’s organised crime at it’s best, he has asked that we hide his identity.

INSIDER: They don’t wake up one morning and decide they’re going to attack a CIT vehicle // the organisers are always the same.

VO: The shooters, foot soldiers and drivers rotate between jobs, and there are always insiders.

INSIDER: They scout the trucks weeks in advance - where they drive, where they pick up.

VO: This clip is of an attempted explosives attack on a Cash Truck. You can see a group of 8 heavily armed men. Here one is carrying a bag believed to contain the explosives. The staff surrendered and the gang made off with just over R10 million

Sam says These are professionals at work.

INSIDER: The attacks are executed with military precision and their shooting is extremely accurate.
KEVIN: Perpatrators are making use of automatic weapons, R5’s R4’s AK47, some of them with armoured piercing rounds
INSIDER: there’s not only police involvement but ex-military members too.

VO: An allegation Lt Netshiunda doesn’t deny.

ROBERT: We cannot sit here and say there is no involvement of police or even military personell // to get access to an R5 rifle, you need to be some how connected.

VO: But just how difficult is it to get explosives? Easy says Nathi. There is an booming black market for it. He agreed to show us just how easy by making a call to a supplier.

INFORMANT: And how much for the Safe stuff?
SUPPLIER: for the safe it’s R3500.
INFORMANT: it’s urgent, very urgent
SUPPLIER: we’ll meet, you’ll give me the R3500 and i’ll give them to you.

VO: Just hours later Nathi made the exchange with the supplier.

This is what R3500 bought. Four catridges of watergel explosives – enough for at least four robberies.

These are commercial explosives used commonly in the mining industry.

Explosives Expert, Dr. Piet Halliday, says once the explosives leave the manufacturer, the controls are not quite as stringent.

PIET: The explosives are accessible, controlling them from a legal point of view depends on people blowing the whistle on these guys. INT 4 M2

VO: But greed often overrides common sense when amateurs try their luck with explosives.

Like the robber in this footage. Watch as he plants the explosives, then he moves away but comes back to check something - just as the safe blows up. A second robber, drags him out and they make a run for it. The police later recovered three fingers at the scene.

But what happens when inexperienced criminals go too far with explosives in an armoured cash truck?

We decided to put a 2007 Cash-in-Transit Load body to the test. This shell is standard; the only difference with newer models is additional technology.

LINK: this is ARnie, he’s got lots of muscle at 3.5 tons, he’s made of 4 mm armoured steel.

VO: Before we see how he holds up, we took a look inside.

PIET: depending on the position of the explosives you might rupture the side or it will burst at the seams.
DEVI: Chances are that ‘s what will happen.
PIET: // that’s the big problem with these guys, they don’t know where to stop – they are not experts. INT 1 M3

VO: Our qualified blast master loaded the explosives in Arnie’s dropsafe. We then took cover in a blast shelter.

LINK: Devi sjoh…nervous laugh

VO: It was over in seconds…. shrapnel went flying through the air, shockwaves can been seen emanating from the blast; and as the dust settled only fragments of the shell remained. This Arnie won’t be back!

DEVI: you have no idea about shrapnel until you actually get here to see the bits and pieces that are left over.
PIET: What this illustrates is that you can’t predict what is going to happen. // what has happened here is quite devastating // It;s very hit and miss for them.

VO: According to Lt. Netshiunda a number of explosives are also coming over our borders

ROBERT: We arrest criminals coming into the country, many of the explosive we have recovered from Zimbabwe at Beitbridge // we believe that maybe other neighbouring countries may also have a hand in this.

KEVIN: IT’s absolutely criminal, but I think the concern is that it is so easy to use explosives in the country and not have consequences. The same people we believe are committing the same crimes over a given period,

VO: But as the criminals adapt their tactics, the security companies are also adapting their strategies says Wahl.

WAHL: one of the things we are doing is reducing the loads on our vehicles, so we manage the risk and we would split the risk on different vehicles.
DEVI: So you’re carrying less money.
WAHL: Yes we do.
WAHL: we are changing and we are deploying new technology to the vehicles to ensure we are staying one jump ahead of crime

VO: James Engelbrecht manufacturers armoured vehicles for the industry. The latest trend is to protect the assets using technology and cash safe reconfiguration, rather than brute force.

JAMES: We try and make it as difficult as possible for anyone to put explosives into the vehicle. And as long as you stay inside the vehicle, you can never say never, but it should be virtually impossible for anyone to come into the vehicle with explosives. To try and attach explosives on the side of this vehicle, is all it does it blows it away.

VO: Only when security staff surrender, can the robbers gain access to plant explosives

LINK: Depending on the amount of explosives used, these armoured vehicles burst at the seams – the real damage is on the inside

VO: But it’s not always a win for the criminals says Wahl.

WAHL: A lot of the cash normally gets damaged when they blow up the vehicle, but also we use some dye stain to secure the cash and to damage the cash so they cannot use it.

VO: With little progress being made and hardly any positive arrests, industry investigators like Sam feel despondent.

INSIDER: After a year of attacks with losses over R150 million, we’re still waiting for a task team assigned.

VO: But Lt Netshiunda says they’re doing their best and are working with Crime Intelligence.

DEVI: you can’t say that you’ve been on top your game, you’re not on top of your game
ROBERT: we cannot say we haven’t been doing nothing. // From a citizen point of view, it looks simple to crack these crimes , it’s a lot more complicated we are dealing with a sophisticated group of criminals here.

VO: Criminals who are crippling the economy - one explosive robbery at a time.


PROMOS

PROMO 1 – 10 seconds
VO: Criminals target cash management systems using black market explosives – but just how safe is it in the hands of amateur robbers
KABOOM!!!


PROMO 2
VO: A new crime trend using explosives in cash robberies across SA see criminals making off with millions.

KEVIN: where there is going to be cash, you are probably going to get explosives, whether it be a safe, a drop safe, whether it be a CIT vehicle or an ATM,
PROMO 3

VO: With explosive robberies on the rise – just how easy is it to get your hands on the illicit goods?

INFORMANT: it’s urgent, very urgent
SUPPLIER: we’ll meet, you’ll give me the R3500 and i’ll give them to you.

VO Carte Blanche investigates a growing black market for explosives.
